rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He reads أن as a subjunctive verbal noun with an omitted preposition, preferably “for making complete coats of mail”; “He commanded him to make” is another estimate.
rows.anchor: مصدرية وهي على إسقاط حرف الجر

rows.speaker: الحوفي وغيره
rows.claim: They allow أن as an explanatory particle, although this requires a preceding sense of speech; some posit an omitted command, but deleting its explanatory verb is unattested.
rows.anchor: وأجاز الحوفي وغيره أن تكون مفسرة ولما كان شرط المفسرة أن يتقدمها معنى القول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: سابغات means coats of mail; it originally described completeness and fullness, then became a conventional name for mail.
rows.anchor: والسابغات الدروع وأصله صفة من السبوغ وهو التمام والكمال فغلب على الدروع

rows.speaker: الشاعر
rows.claim: An anonymous poetic line uses سابغات for protective mail.
rows.anchor: لا سابغات ولا جأواء باسلة تقي المنون لدى إستيفاء آجال

rows.speaker: الشاعر
rows.claim: Another poem uses the plural سوابغ for white mail that arrows cannot pierce.
rows.anchor: عليها أسود ضاريات لبوسهم سوابغ بيض لا تخرقها النبل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: No omitted noun such as “coats” is needed before سابغات; this does not refute the rule against deleting an adjective’s noun unless the adjective is distinctive.
rows.anchor: فلا حاجة إلى تقدير موصوف أي دروعا سابغات ولا يرد هذا نقصا

rows.speaker: قارئ
rows.claim: A reading replaces sīn with ṣād in صابغات, assimilating the sound to the following ghayn.
rows.anchor: بإبدال السين صادا لأجل الغين

rows.speaker: الراغب
rows.claim: Rāghib explains سرد as interlacing or stitching something rough and thick; the term is extended to the making of iron links.
rows.anchor: السرد نسج في الأصل كما قال الراغب خرز ما يخشن ويغلظ

rows.speaker: الشماخ
rows.claim: Al-Shammākh’s phrase سرد العنان uses سرد for successive stringing or interlacing, evidence for the root sense.
rows.anchor: قال الشماخ فظلت سراعا خيلنا في بيوتكم كما تابعت سرد العنان الخوارز

rows.speaker: البحر
rows.claim: Al-Baḥr glosses سرد as following one thing with another of its kind; a mail coat is linked because its rings follow one another.
rows.anchor: وفي البحر هو إتباع الشيء بالشيء من جنسه ويقال للدرع مسرودة

rows.speaker: الشاعر
rows.claim: A poem describes two coats as مسرودتان, exemplifying mail formed by linked rings.
rows.anchor: وعليهما مسرودتان قضاهما داؤد أو صنع السوابغ تبع

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās, in reports cited by al-Ṭabarī, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abī Ḥātim, explains the command as making the rings proportionate.
rows.anchor: وإبن عباس فيما أخرجه عنه إبن جرير وإبن المنذر وإبن أبي حاتم من طرق بالحلق

rows.speaker: ابن زيد
rows.claim: Ibn Zayd says to avoid rings so small that the armor is weak and so large that gaps leave its wearer exposed.
rows.anchor: لا تعملها صغيرة فتضعف فلا يقوى الدرع على الدفاع

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وقتادة ومجاهد
rows.claim: A second report from Ibn ʿAbbās, also attributed to Qatāda and Mujāhid, takes سرد as rivets: size them to fit the holes, neither too thin to hold nor too thick to tear the rings.
rows.anchor: وجاء في رواية أخرى عن إبن عباس تفسيرها بالمسامير وروى ذلك عن قتادة ومجاهد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī questions the rivet explanation because softened iron could have its ring ends fused like wax or dough, making a stronger join without rivets; if the report is sound, David may have joined rings without fusing them.
rows.anchor: ويبعد هذا أن إلانة الحديد له عليه السلام بحيث كان كالشمع والعجين يغني عن التسمير

rows.speaker: البقاعي
rows.claim: Al-Biqāʿī reports an unnamed observer’s claim that David’s armor had no rivets; al-Ālūsī dismisses it because the informant is unidentified.
rows.anchor: ما نقل عن البقاعي أنه قال

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another gloss limits armor-making to the amount needed for a livelihood, leaving the rest of David’s time for worship; it fits the following command.
rows.anchor: لا تصرف جميع أوقاتك فيه بل مقدار ما يحصل به القوت

rows.speaker: قتادة
rows.claim: A report from Qatāda says David was the first to make ringed mail; before him, armor was made of solid plates.
rows.anchor: وحكى أنه عليه السلام أول من صنع الدرع حلقا وكانت قبل صفائح وروى ذلك عن قتادة

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqātil reports that, when David ruled Israel, an angel disguised as a man said he was virtuous except that he lived from the treasury; David prayed to learn a trade, was taught armor-making, prospered, and sold a coat for 1,000 dirhams.
rows.anchor: وعن مقاتل أنه عليه السلام حين ملك على بني إسرائيل يخرج متنكرا فيسأل الناس عن حاله

rows.speaker: ابن شوذب
rows.claim: Ibn Shawdhab reports that David made one coat daily and sold it for 6,000 dirhams, keeping 2,000 for his household and spending 4,000 to feed Israelites fine white bread.
rows.anchor: عن إبن شوذب قال : كان داؤد عليه السلام يرفع

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another account says David sold each coat for 4,000 dirhams, supporting his family and giving alms to the poor.
rows.anchor: وقيل : كان يبيع الدرع بأربعة آلاف

rows.speaker: الصادق
rows.claim: Al-Ṣādiq is cited in Majmaʿ al-Bayān as saying David made 360 coats and sold them for 360,000 dirhams, becoming independent of the public treasury.
rows.anchor: وفي مجمع البيان عن الصادق رضي الله تعالى عنه أنه عمل ثلثمائة وستين درعا

rows.speaker: الخفاجي
rows.claim: Al-Khafājī takes the address as David and his family, understood by implication from the mention of David.
rows.anchor: وهم وإن لم يجر لهم ذكر يفهمون على ما قال الخفاجي إلتزاما من ذكره

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another view makes David alone the addressee, with the plural form honoring him.
rows.anchor: وجوز أن يكون خطابا له عليه السلام خاصة على سبيل التعظيم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Either way, the apparent command is to do righteous deeds generally; if addressed only to David, it is not merely a command to make flawless armor.
rows.anchor: وأياما كان فالظاهر أنه أمر بالعمل الصالح مطلقا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s seeing their deeds means He will recompense them, explaining the command or its binding force and motivating obedience through encouragement and warning.
rows.anchor: فأجازيكم به وهو تعليل للأمر أو لوجوب الإمتثال به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: No sinful soul bears the sin of another; each soul bears its own burden.
rows.anchor: أي لا تحمل نفس آثمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This does not conflict with 29:13: misleaders carry their own sins plus sins caused by misleading others, not the actual sins of those followers; the added burden is their own incitement and causation.
rows.anchor: ولا منافاة بين هذا وقوله تعالى في سورة العنكبوت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A مثقلة is a soul weighed down by sins; it calls someone to take or lighten its burden, the sin that oppresses it.
rows.anchor: أي نفس أثقلتها الأوزار

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: An alternative construes إلى حملها as a call to bear the burden of its load.
rows.anchor: وقيل : أي إلى حمل حملها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: No one responds by carrying any part of the soul’s burden; the initial negation concerns voluntary, generous assistance and rebuts sinners’ claim that others would carry their sins.
rows.anchor: نفي للحمل الإختياري تكرما من نفس الحامل

rows.speaker: الوليد بن المغيرة
rows.claim: The reported occasion is that al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīra told believers to reject Muḥammad and promised to carry their sins; the verse was revealed in response.
rows.anchor: أن الوليد بن المغيرة قال لقوم من المؤمنين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The second clause denies carrying even after the burdened soul asks, thus covering voluntary and forced carrying, every kind of burden and any possible carrier; if none is compelled after a request, none is compelled without one.
rows.anchor: وهذا نفي للحمل بعد الطلب من الوازرة أعم من أن يكون إختيارا أو جبرا

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: One distinction is that the first clause denies transferring the entire burden, while the second denies even lessening it.
rows.anchor: إن في الأولى نفي حمل جميع الوزر بحيث يتعرى منه المحمول عنه وفي الثاني نفي التخفيف

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another distinction says the first clause denies forced carrying and the second voluntary carrying; the objection is that the wording should then reverse these cases and explicitly name coercion.
rows.anchor: إن الأول نفي الحمل إجبارا والثاني نفي له إختيارا

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: A further distinction assigns complete justice to the first clause and the absence of any refuge from that day’s terror to the second; al-Ālūsī prefers his broader reading.
rows.anchor: الجملة الأولى كما دلت على أن المثقل بالذنوب

rows.speaker: بعض الأفاضل
rows.claim: An objection asks why the wording specifies a sinful soul instead of saying that no soul bears another’s burden, which would state the generality more explicitly and concisely.
rows.anchor: عدم حمل الغير على الغير عام في النفس الآثمة وغير الآثمة فلم خص بالآثمة

rows.speaker: بعض الأفاضل
rows.claim: The reply is that the discussion concerns sinners punished for their own sins, not for deeds committed by someone else.
rows.anchor: وجوابه أن الكلام في أرباب الأوزار المعذبين لبيان أن عذابهم

rows.speaker: بعض الأفاضل
rows.claim: A second objection asks how وزر can follow تزر without redundancy, since lexicons define وزر as bearing a heavy thing or sin; the proposed answer calls it grammatical tajrīd.
rows.anchor: أن معنى وزر حمل الوزر لا مطلق الحمل على ما في النهاية الأثيرية

rows.speaker: بعض الأفاضل
rows.claim: A third objection asks what benefit وازرة adds if the active participle is already implied by تزر; the response is that it presents the soul as already characterized by bearing, and an indefinite participle under negation also generalizes.
rows.anchor: أن ( وازرة ) يفهم من تزر كما يفهم ضارب من يضرب

rows.speaker: بعض الأفاضل
rows.claim: The scholar’s answer is that an active participle marks an established quality concurrent with the action; its indefinite use under negation adds generality, contrary to al-Taftāzānī’s claim that the participle adds little.
rows.anchor: وهذه فائدة جليلة ويزيدها جلالة إستفادة العموم إذا أورد أسم الفاعل نكرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī says the wording needs no grammatical tajrīd: lexicons define وزر يزر as bearing a burden.
rows.anchor: وفي القاموس وزره كوعده وزرا بالكسر حمله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Together the clauses state the general rule raised in the first objection while preserving added benefit in their separate phrasing.
rows.anchor: وأنت تعلم أنه من مجموع الجملتين يستفاد

rows.speaker: أبو السمال عن طلحة وإبراهيم عن الكسائي
rows.claim: They read لا تحمل with second-person feminine tāʾ and a kasra on mīm; شيء is accusative, and the subject is the person called: if a burdened soul asks someone to carry, that person carries none of it.
rows.anchor: عن الكسائي ( لا تحمل ) بفتح التاء المثناة من فوق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The implied subject of كان is the person summoned, even if that person is related to the caller; this is more natural than making the caller the subject.
rows.anchor: والأول أحسن لأن الداعي هو المثقلة بعينه

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya instead makes the subject of كان the caller, so the phrase means even if the caller is related to the person called.
rows.anchor: إبن عطية : اسم كان ضمير الداعي

rows.speaker: أبو حيان
rows.claim: Abū Ḥayyān says the masculine pronoun follows the meaning of مثقلة, which denotes any person, not only a grammatically feminine individual; al-Ālūsī says the point is evident.
rows.anchor: وقول أبي حيان ذكر الضمير حملا على المعنى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This is a fresh statement identifying those who heed the warnings: only those who fear their Lord benefit, unlike the rebellious and obstinate.
rows.anchor: إستئناف مسوق لبيان من يتعظ بما ذكر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: بالغيب can mean fearing God while unseen from His punishment, while alone away from people, or fearing punishment that is itself unseen; the phrase is circumstantial of the subject or object.
rows.anchor: أي يخشونه تعالى غائبين عن عذابه سبحانه أو عن الناس في خلواتهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Establishing prayer means observing it properly and making it a raised beacon and standard.
rows.anchor: وأقاموا الصلاة أي راعوها كما ينبغي وجعلوها منارا منصوبا وعلما مرفوعا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The difference in verbal forms is explained by the earlier discussion of 35:9, “God sends the winds, then they stir a cloud.”
rows.anchor: في قوله تعالى ( الله الذي أرسل الرياح فتثير سحابا )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: تزكى means purifying oneself from sins and their stains by being affected by these warnings.
rows.anchor: تطهر من أدناس الأوزار والمعاصي بالتأثر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Purification benefits only the person who undertakes it, just as sin’s defilement harms only its agent; purification includes fearing God and establishing prayer, so the verse reinforces and urges both.
rows.anchor: لإقتصار نفعه عليها كما أن من تدنس بها لا يتدنس إلا عليها والتزكي شامل للخشية

rows.speaker: العباس عن أبي عمرو
rows.claim: He reads ومن يزكى فإنما يزكي with yāʾ and a doubled zāy in both verbs, from يتزكى by assimilation of tāʾ into zāy, as in يذكرون.
rows.anchor: عن أبي عمرو ( ومن يزكى فإنما يزكي )

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود وطلحة
rows.claim: Ibn Masʿūd and Ṭalḥa read ومن أزكى, assimilating tāʾ into zāy and adding a connecting hamza at the start; Ṭalḥa also reads فإنما تزكى with assimilation.
rows.anchor: إبن مسعود وطلحة ( ومن أزكى ) بإدغام التاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The return is to God alone, with no other independently or jointly, and He rewards those who purify themselves with the best recompense.
rows.anchor: لا إلى أحد غيره إستقلالا أو إشتراكا فيجازيهم على تزكيهم أحسن الجزاء

rows.speaker: الطيبي
rows.claim: Al-Ṭībī takes the living and dead as anaphoric references to believers who accepted the message after the mission and disbelievers who persisted arrogantly.
rows.anchor: تمثيل آخر للمؤمنين الذين دخلوا في الدين بعد البعثة والكافرين الذين أصروا

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another view takes the living and dead to mean scholars and the ignorant.
rows.anchor: فالتعريف كما قال الطيبي للعهد وقيل : للعلماء والجهلاء

rows.speaker: الثعالبي
rows.claim: Al-Thaʿālibī makes the blind and sighted, rather than the living and dead, the two figures for believers and disbelievers; al-Ālūsī rejects this.
rows.anchor: والثعالبي جعل الأعمى والبصير مثلين لهما وليس بذاك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God makes whom He wills hear and enables them to perceive sounds.
rows.anchor: أي سمعه ويجعله مدركا للأصوات

rows.speaker: الخفاجي وغيره
rows.claim: Al-Khafājī and others suggest the hearing is attentive acceptance and reflection on God’s signs.
rows.anchor: وقال الخفاجي وغيره : ولعل في الآية ما يقتضي

words: وما أنت بمسمع من في القبور
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The grave image extends the comparison of the obstinate disbelievers with the dead and despairs the Prophet of their conversion; the emphatic bāʾ is extra.
rows.anchor: ترشيح لتمثيل المصرين على الكفر بالأموات وأشباع في إقناطه عليه الصلاة والسلام

words: وما أنت بمسمع من في القبور
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The negated hearing is ordinary, effective hearing, not an absolute denial that the dead can hear; the report about the well victims describes an extraordinary event, like God’s attribution of the Prophet’s throwing to Himself.
rows.anchor: والمراد بالسماع هنا ما أريد به في سابقه ولا يأبى إرادة السماع المعروف ماورد في حديث القليب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The analogies progress from the two seas (35:12) to blind and sighted with darkness, light, shade, and heat, then to living and dead, intensifying the contrast and adding the loss of external light before reaching death.
rows.anchor: وما ألطف نظم هذه التمثيلات فقد شبه المؤمن والكافر أولا بالبحرين وفضل البحر الأجاج

rows.speaker: الطيبي
rows.claim: Al-Ṭībī says omission of the emphatic لا in the blind/sighted comparison prepares for the next living/dead comparison and explains its repeated opening; later pairs have لا because they stand as independent figures for truth, falsehood, reward, and punishment.
rows.anchor: ذكر الطيبي أن إخلاء الثاني من لا المؤكدة

rows.speaker: الطيبي
rows.claim: The inserted لا does not mean different kinds of darkness fail to equal one another; the intended contrasts are darkness with light, shade with heat, and living with dead.
rows.anchor: أن الظلمات لا تساوي النور والظل لا يساوي الحرور

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya says each لا implies repetition before the paired noun, with the initial terms standing for the omitted second terms; al-Ālūsī says treating لا as emphatic makes this deletion unnecessary.
rows.anchor: وزعم إبن عطية أن دخول لا على نية التكرار

rows.speaker: الإمام
rows.claim: The Imām says لا is repeated because darkness and light, and shade and heat, are opposites; shade means absence of heat and cold, whereas one person can be sighted and later blind.
rows.anchor: وقال الإمام : كررت لا فيما كررت لتأكيد المنافاة

rows.speaker: الإمام
rows.claim: The Imām says life and death are more completely opposed than sight and blindness: sighted and blind may share perception, while the dead differs from the living in its very reality.
rows.anchor: وإن كانا كالأعمى والبصير من حيث أن الجسم الواحد قد يكون حيا ثم يعرض له الموت

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: One explanation says لا is omitted from the first pair because the listener readily understands the intended contrast, then repeated afterward.
rows.anchor: وقيل لم تكر قيل وكررت بعد لأن المخاطب في أول الكلام لا يقصر في فهم المراد

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another explanation says later لا prevents reading the phrase as denying equality between the combined groups, and the last repetition marks special emphasis.
rows.anchor: وقيل كررت فيما عدا الأخير لأنه لو قيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The blind precedes the sighted because it represents the disbeliever, present before the call; darkness likewise precedes light because falsehood existed until the Prophet’s mission erased it.
rows.anchor: وقدم الأعمى على البصير مع أن البصير أشرف لأنه إشارة إلى الكافر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Shade precedes heat, unlike the prior less-noble-first pairs, because of its affinity with blindness and darkness or the precedence of mercy, and to maintain the verse ending.
rows.anchor: ولم يقدم الحرور على الظل ليكون على طرز ما سبق من تقديم غير الأشرف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The living precede the dead because they represent believers after the message and the dead represent those persisting in disbelief; the next clause about whom God makes hear supports this.
rows.anchor: وقدم الأحياء على الأموات ولم يعكس الأمر ليوافق الأولين في تقديم غير الأشرف

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another explanation says earlier pairs put nonexistence first, but here death follows life because the intended dead are those who first had life, as the grave image confirms.
rows.anchor: وقيل قدم ما قدم فيما عدا الأخير لأنه عدم وله مرتبة السبق

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: A further explanation says placing the less noble first does not diminish the superior one’s rank, even though the order signals their difference.
rows.anchor: وقيل أن تقديم غير الأشرف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fire can be surmounted by smoke and horsemen’s turbans by dust, illustrating how what seems subordinate may be placed above what is more noble.
rows.anchor: فالنار يعلوها الدخان وربما يعلو الغبار عمائم الفرسان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Darkness is plural and light singular because falsehood has many forms while truth is one.
rows.anchor: وجمع الظلمات مع أفراد النور لتعدد فنون الباطل وإتحاد الحق

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another explanation says darkness can occupy separate places with light between them, whereas this world’s many lights unify beyond their separate locations.
rows.anchor: وقيل لأن الظلمة قد تتعدد فتكون في محال قد تخلل بينهما نور

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Living and dead are plural because there are multiple referents; blind and sighted remain singular to express a generic class and preserve cadence.
rows.anchor: وجمع الأحياء والأموات على بابه لتعدد المشبه بهما ولم يجمع الأعمى والبصير

rows.speaker: الأشهب والحسن
rows.claim: Al-Ashhab and al-Ḥasan read بمسمع من with an iḍāfa construction.
rows.anchor: الحسن ( بمسمع من ) بالإضافة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase means “some of the people, beasts, and livestock,” or “some among them are varied in color,” like 2:8; it coordinates with the preceding sentence and follows its syntax.
rows.anchor: أي ومنهم بعض مختلف ألوانه أو بعضهم مختلف ألوانه على ما ذكروا

rows.speaker: إرشاد العقل السليم
rows.claim: Irshād says nominal clauses describe ongoing color variation, unlike the preceding verbal clause for fruits emerging; only fruit variation is tied to a prompting question about seeing.
rows.anchor: أن إيراد الجملتين أسميتين مع مشاركتهما لما قبلهما من الجملة الفعلية

rows.speaker: البحر
rows.claim: Al-Baḥr says the question about seeing seeks agreement about something especially obvious; al-Ālūsī notes this conflicts with Irshād’s claim that fruit variation is less obvious.
rows.anchor: بخلاف أحوال الجبال والناس وغيرهما فإنها مشاهدة غنية عن التأمل

rows.speaker: الزهري
rows.claim: Al-Zuhrī reads الدواب with a light bāʾ to avoid two vowelless consonants, as some readers hamza ولا الضالين for the same reason.
rows.anchor: وقرأ الزهري ( والدواب ) بتخفيف الباء

rows.speaker: ابن السميقع
rows.claim: Ibn al-Sumayqiʿ reads ألوانها with feminine agreement.
rows.anchor: وقرأ إبن السميقع ( ألوانها )

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: كذلك is an accusative adjective for the verbal noun of مختلف: variation of the same kind as with fruits and mountains; it completes the preceding clause, and reciters agree that stopping here is good.
rows.anchor: في محل نصب صفة لمصدر مختلف المؤكد والتقدير مختلف إختلافا كائنا كذلك

words: إنما يخشى الله من عباده العلماء
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The scholars’ fear completes 35:18 by naming those among people who fear God, after indicating the honor of fear, the ugliness of its opposite, warning the heedless, and recalling divine power.
rows.anchor: إنما تنذر الذين يخشون ربهم بالغيب

words: إنما يخشى الله من عباده العلماء
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, the clause follows the distinction between people’s inner ranks by analogy and their outward ranks by direct description, giving each kind of difference its fitting explanation.
rows.anchor: أو بعد بيان إختلاف طبقات الناس وتباين مراتبهم أما في الأوصاف المعنوية

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another parsing makes كذلك the predicate of an omitted subject: the matter is as described; the next clause shifts indirectly to God’s friends and indicates that knowledge brings fitting fear.
rows.anchor: وقيل ( كذلك ) في موضع رفع خبر مبتدأ محذوف

rows.speaker: صاحب الكشف
rows.claim: Ṣāḥib al-Kashf says the nominative, omitted-subject parsing is clearer because it creates a decisive transition in the discourse.
rows.anchor: قال صاحب الكشف : والرفع أظهر ليكون من فصل الخطاب

rows.speaker: ابن عطية
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAṭiyya attaches كذلك to the following clause as its cause: reflecting on God’s creations and their varied colors leads scholars to fear Him.
rows.anchor: وقال إبن عطية يحتمل أن يكون ( كذلك ) متعلقا بما بعده

rows.speaker: السمين
rows.claim: Al-Samīn rejects that attachment because إنما cannot govern backward and because reciters stop at كذلك.
rows.anchor: ورده السمين بأن إنما لا يعمل ما بعدها فيما قبلها وبأن الوقف على كذلك

rows.speaker: الخفاجي
rows.claim: Al-Khafājī approves al-Samīn’s objection but says it does not weaken the omitted-subject reading, since that reading does not make إنما govern backward and the stopping rule does not settle it.
rows.anchor: وأرتضاه الخفاجي وقال : وبه ظهر ضعف ما قيل

rows.speaker: ابن جريج
rows.claim: Ibn Jurayj, transmitted by Ibn al-Mundhir, says that just as livestock differ in color, people differ in their fear of God.
rows.anchor: أخرج إبن المنذر عن إبن جريج أنه قال في الآية كما أختلفت هذه الأنعام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ālūsī calls Ibn Jurayj’s comparison weak; he considers the majority reading most apparent and the omitted-subject transition more precise and subtle.
rows.anchor: وهذا عندى ضعيف والأظهر ما عليه الجمهور وما قيل أدق وألطف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The scholars here know God, His fitting attributes, actions, and affairs, not merely grammar or morphology; the more one knows God, the more one fears Him.
rows.anchor: والمراد بالعلماء العالمون بالله عزوجل وبما يليق به من صفاته الجليلة

words: إنما يخشى الله من عباده العلماء
rows.speaker: عطاء عن موسى
rows.claim: Al-Dārimī transmits from ʿAṭāʾ that Moses asked who was wisest, richest, and most God-fearing; God said the most fearful is the one who knows Him best.
rows.anchor: روى الدارمي عن عطاء قال : قال موسى عليه السلام

words: إنما يخشى الله من عباده العلماء
rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: A sound Prophetic report says, I am the most God-fearing and most pious of you.
rows.anchor: وصح عنه صلى الله عليه وسلم أنه قال أنا أخشاكم لله وأتقاكم له

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās, in reports cited by Ibn al-Mundhir and al-Ṭabarī, glosses the scholars as those who know God has power over everything.
rows.anchor: فسر إبن عباس كما أخرج عنه إبن المنذر وإبن جرير

words: إنما يخشى الله من عباده العلماء
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fronting God as object identifies the people who fear Him—the scholars; later order would emphasize God as the only one feared, as in 9:18, which is not the present point.
rows.anchor: وتقديم المفعول لأن المقصود بيان الخاشين والأخبار بأنهم العلماء خاصة دون غيرهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This wording implicitly rebukes obstinate unbelievers as ignorant of God and His attributes, explaining why they neither fear Him nor dread His punishment.
rows.anchor: بل يقتضي الأول ليكون تعريضا بالمنذرين المصرين على الكفر والعناد

words: إنما يخشى الله من عباده العلماء
rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some deny that إنما restricts the claim to scholars, but al-Ālūsī dismisses this denial.
rows.anchor: وأنكر بعضهم إفادة ( إنما ) هنا للحصر

words: إنما يخشى الله من عباده العلماء
rows.speaker: عمر بن عبد العزيز وأبو حنيفة
rows.claim: A reading attributed to ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz and Abū Ḥanīfa puts God in the nominative and scholars in the accusative; Ibn al-Jazarī attacks it, and Abū Ḥayyān doubts its authenticity.
rows.anchor: وروى عن عمر بن عبدالعزيز وأبي حنيفة رضي الله تعالى عنهما أنهما قرءا

words: إنما يخشى الله من عباده العلماء
rows.speaker: الزمخشري
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī mentions the anomalous reading; Abū al-Qāsim Yūsuf ibn ʿAlī ibn Junāda also records it from Abū Ḥaywa in al-Kāmil.
rows.anchor: وإنما ذكرها الزمخشري وذكرها عن أبي حيوة أبو القاسم يوسف بن علي بن جنادة

words: إنما يخشى الله من عباده العلماء
rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: One view takes fear metaphorically as reverence, since what is revered inspires awe; another takes it as choosing, as in the poem about selecting one’s cousins.
rows.anchor: وخرجت على أن الخشية مجاز عن التعظيم بعلاقة اللزوم فإن المعظم يكون مهيبا

words: إنما يخشى الله من عباده العلماء
rows.speaker: الشاعر
rows.claim: The poem’s phrase خشيت بني عمي uses خشيت in the sense of choosing or selecting.
rows.anchor: وقيل الخشية ترد بمعنى الإختيار كقوله خشيت بني عمي فلم أر مثلهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s might obliges fear because it signals power to punish; forgiveness and mercy are attributed only to one capable of punishment.
rows.anchor: تعليل لوجوب الخشية لأن العزة دالة على كمال القدرة على الإنتقام

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another view treats غفور as rhetorical completion (takmīl), paralleling a verse by al-Ghanawī cited earlier.
rows.anchor: من باب التكميل نظير ما في بيت الغنوي المذكور آنفا

words: إنما يخشى الله من عباده العلماء
rows.speaker: أبو بكر الصديق
rows.claim: Some transmitted reports say the verse was revealed concerning Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq, whose fear of God became visibly apparent.
rows.anchor: والآية على ما في بعض الآثار نزلت في أبي بكر الصديق رضي الله تعالى عنه
